pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 11–13 — round numbers and measures to an appropriate degree of accuracy, including to a specified number of decimal places or significant figures.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): 'round numbers and measures to an appropriate degree of accuracy (e.g. to a number of decimal places or significant figures).'
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): builds on 5.NBT.A.4 (round decimals to any place); significant figures are not a named CCSS strand but appear in science/measurement and high-school modelling (N.Q). Emphasis in US is on appropriate precision.
• Operational details: Extend nearness-based rounding to (a) a stated number of decimal places and (b) significant figures. The key new idea is IDENTIFYING significant figures — the first significant figure is the first non-zero digit; leading zeros are not significant; trailing/placeholder zeros hold magnitude. Round using the digit AFTER the last significant/required place (midpoint rule), then restore place value with zeros (2 sig figs of 34,700 → 35,000). Choose accuracy to suit context.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 11): 'Round 3.4567 to 2 dp.' Tier B: 'Round 0.004982 to 2 significant figures.' Tier C: 'Round 34,750 to 2 sig figs and explain why the answer needs its zeros.'
bestPractices: Teach significant-figure identification first: the first sig fig is the first non-zero digit; leading zeros never count; placeholder zeros preserve magnitude
Keep rounding as a nearness/midpoint decision, then RESTORE place value with the right zeros (35,000, not 35)
Contrast dp and sig figs on the same number so pupils see they can differ (0.004982 to 2 dp = 0.00 vs to 2 sf = 0.0050)
Attend to the round-up cascade and trailing zeros that record precision (2.988 to 2 dp → 2.99; 1.998 to 2 dp → 2.00)
Link accuracy to context — choose dp/sf appropriate to the measurement's precision
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart marking the rounding place and the deciding next digit
Number line with the two candidate rounded values and the midpoint
Side-by-side dp-vs-sf comparison of the same number
commonMisconceptions: Counting leading zeros as significant (0.0049 seen as 4 sig figs)
Dropping the placeholder zeros after rounding to sig figs (35,000 written as 35)
Confusing decimal places with significant figures
Truncating instead of rounding, or double-rounding through intermediate digits
Losing the trailing zero that records the rounded precision (2.90 written as 2.9 when 2 dp is required)

learn.summary: For ages 11–13: round numbers and measures to a stated number of decimal places or significant figures, and choose an accuracy appropriate to context. The central new skill is identifying significant figures (first sig fig = first non-zero digit; leading zeros never count; placeholder/trailing zeros do real work holding magnitude and recording precision), then making a single nearness/midpoint rounding decision and restoring place value with zeros (34,750 to 2 sf → 35,000, not 35).

activities.title: Highlight the significant figures, round once, rebuild the size
feedback: If a learner writes 34,750 to 2 sf as 35, ask them to say the value aloud — 35 is thirty-five, not thirty-five thousand; the thousands zeros are load-bearing placeholders.
If leading zeros are counted (treating 0.004982 as having significant leading zeros), re-establish that counting begins at the first non-zero digit (the 4); leading zeros only hold place.

If a learner rounds digit-by-digit (e.g. 3.1449 to 2 dp: 3.1449 → 3.145 → 3.15), show that only the digit immediately after the required place matters (here the 4), so the decision is made once and gives 3.14; chain rounding made the answer drift to 3.15.
If the trailing zero is lost (0.0050 written as 0.005, or 2.90 to 2 dp written as 2.9), point out the final zero records the rounded precision and is required.
activities.rationale: The curriculum goal here is identifying significant figures and restoring place value, which is the step learners find new and error-prone. Making the highlighting, the single deciding digit, and the zero-restoration visible is intended to target the conflation between dp and sf and the 'drop the zeros' error. A live sig-fig highlighter, a number-line midpoint marker, and a dp/sf toggle on the same number are optional interaction examples that may make the mechanism concrete; they are not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils round numbers and measures to an appropriate degree of accuracy, including a specified number of decimal places or significant figures.
learnerActions: Take a number such as 34,750 and decide to round it to 2 significant figures.
Mark the counted significant digits (the 3 and the 4), confirming you start at the first non-zero digit.

Identify the single deciding digit immediately after the last required place (the 7) and place the number on a number line between its two candidate rounded values (34,000 and 35,000) and their midpoint (34,500); decide the round-up in one step.
Reassemble the answer as 35,000, writing in the placeholder zeros that keep the number in the thousands — do NOT stop at 35.

Now take 0.004982 and round to 2 significant figures: cross out the leading zeros as 'not significant', count the 4 and 9, apply the deciding digit (8) so 49 rounds up to 50, and write 0.0050 — keeping the front zeros for magnitude and the trailing zero for precision.
Repeat 0.004982 rounded to 2 decimal places (= 0.00) and place both answers side by side to see that dp and sf give genuinely different results.
activities.intendedInsight: Significant figures are counted from the first non-zero digit; zeros can be placeholders that hold a number's size or trailing zeros that record precision, so they cannot simply be dropped. Rounding is one nearness decision based on the next digit, after which place value must be restored.

activities.title: Contrast decimal places with significant figures on one number
feedback: If both methods give the same answer, check where the first significant figure is. With the same count (e.g. 2 dp and 2 sf), the answers agree when the first non-zero digit is in the tenths place (e.g. 0.364 → 0.36 both ways). They differ for numbers with leading zeros after the decimal point (0.004982) or with digits before the decimal point (3.14159, 47,320).
If a learner says the rules are 'the same', show 0.004982: 2 dp = 0.00 but 2 sf = 0.0050.
activities.rationale: Contrasting dp and sf on the same number is intended to address the named dp-vs-sf confusion. Presenting the comparison explicitly may help learners see that the two instructions are not interchangeable.
learnerActions: Pick a single number (e.g. 0.004982) and round it both to 2 decimal places and to 2 significant figures.
Record the two answers side by side (0.00 vs 0.0050) and write a sentence explaining why they differ.
Do the same for a large number such as 47,320: to 2 sf it is 47,000 (zeros needed), and note how that differs from a decimal-place instruction.
State in your own words when leading zeros are ignored and when zeros must be kept.
activities.intendedInsight: Decimal places and significant figures are different rules: dp counts from the decimal point, while sf counts from the first non-zero digit. The difference is most striking with leading zeros and with large numbers that need placeholder zeros, but they also differ for ordinary numbers (3.14159 is 3.14 to 2 dp and 3.1 to 2 sf). The same number can give very different rounded values under each.

activities.title: Choose and justify an appropriate degree of accuracy
feedback: If the justification ignores magnitude, prompt: does your rounded answer still describe roughly the same quantity as the original?
If a learner cannot name the deciding digit, revisit that only the digit immediately after the required place determines the round.
activities.rationale: The standards emphasise choosing accuracy appropriate to context (US N.Q; UK 'appropriate degree of accuracy'). Requiring spoken or written justification is intended to build reasoning beyond procedural execution. A short mentor-style challenge can surface the 'drop the zeros' and 'leading zeros count' errors during teaching; this is one useful format, not the only way to teach the procedure.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils round numbers and measures to an appropriate degree of accuracy, including a specified number of decimal places or significant figures.
Rounding to accuracy builds on 5.NBT.A.4 (round decimals to any place); appropriate precision is emphasised in high-school modelling (N.Q).
learnerActions: Given a context such as measuring a room's length, decide whether rounding to 2 decimal places or 2 significant figures is more appropriate, and explain why.
Explain to a partner (or in writing) why 47,320 to 2 sf needs its zeros on the end but 47 to 2 sf would not.
Respond to a challenge like: 'You rounded 34,750 to 2 significant figures and wrote 35 — convince me that is the right size.'
Justify which single digit decided each of your roundings and why the remaining digits did not matter.
activities.intendedInsight: Accuracy should suit the precision of the measurement or context, and learners should be able to justify both the rounded value's size and the choice of dp vs sf.

activities.title: Consolidation: quick-check rounding problems
feedback: For 0.004621 to 2 sf, confirm the answer is 0.0046 (the 4 and 6 are the sig figs); 0.00 would come from confusing sf with 2 dp.
For 47,320 to 2 sf, confirm 47,000; an answer of 47 has lost its magnitude.
For 1.998 to 2 dp, note the cascade carries to 2.00 and the trailing zeros must be written.
For 0.004982 to 2 sf, confirm 0.0050; the 0.00 option reflects the dp-vs-sf confusion.
activities.rationale: Short closed-response items can consolidate and check outcomes efficiently, including with a deliberate distractor exposing the dp/sf confusion. Such items check outcomes rather than build the identification skill, so they suit practice after the construction activities rather than instead of them.
learnerActions: Round 0.004982 to 2 significant figures, choosing from answers that include the dp-confusion value 0.00 so you can check you avoid it (the correct value is 0.0050).
Round 2.988 to 2 dp (→ 2.99, a simple round-up) and 1.998 to 2 dp (→ 2.00, where the round-up carries through several places and the trailing zeros must be written).
activities.intendedInsight: After building the identification skill, learners can reliably apply dp and sf rounding, including the round-up cascade and placeholder/trailing zeros, in short targeted items.

constraints: Teach significant-figure identification before rounding to sf: the first sig fig is the first non-zero digit, leading zeros never count, and placeholder/trailing zeros hold magnitude and record precision.
Treat rounding as a single nearness/midpoint decision using only the digit immediately after the required place; avoid digit-by-digit chain rounding, which can make the answer drift.
Always restore place value with zeros after rounding large numbers to sf (35,000 not 35; 47,000 not 47) and keep trailing zeros that record precision (2.90, 0.0050).
Contrast dp and sf on the same number so learners see the rules diverge, especially on leading zeros and large magnitudes.
Closed-response/quick-check items check outcomes and do not, on their own, build significant-figure identification; use them to consolidate after construction work, not instead of it.
A single static worked example illustrates one case but cannot cover arbitrary numbers or let a learner test the dp-vs-sf divergence interactively; use it as a reference, not the whole task.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Both listed sources carry verified:false in the original row; their claims are cited as supporting pedagogical/curriculum content, not as evidence that any activity was tested or that one format is more effective than another.

sourceClaims were trimmed to [] on activities whose rationale concerns only the teaching method or assessment format (the contrast activity and the consolidation activity), because the KS3 claim supports those curriculum topics but not the efficacy of those specific formats. The KS3 claim is retained where a rationale directly states curriculum content, and both claims are retained for the appropriate-accuracy activity where the standards' emphasis is directly invoked.

The original source summary noted that significant figures are not a named CCSS strand but appear in science/measurement and high-school modelling (N.Q); the US emphasis is on appropriate precision rather than named sig-fig procedures. Preserved as context.

The legacy row's claim that '3D adds nothing' to this one-dimensional symbolic task was removed as an unsupported universal; 3D was simply not adopted as a format here, without asserting it can never help.

probeDeeper: Which single digit decided each rounding, and why did the rest not matter?
Why is 0.0046 to 2sf, not 0.00 — which zeros count and which don't?
Why does 47,320 to 2sf need the zeros on the end but 47 to 2sf wouldn't?
For measuring a room, would you round the length to 2 decimal places or 2 sig figs — why?

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts leading zeros as significant figures — rounds 0.004621 to 2sf as 0.00 or 0.0046 treated as 4 sf.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that significant figures start at the first non-zero digit (the 4), so the 4 and 6 are the two sig figs; leading zeros only hold place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Significant-figure count starts at the decimal point or at the first zero, not the first non-zero digit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Chain / digit-by-digit rounding — rounds 3.14159 stepwise (→3.1416→3.142→3.14) or rounds each digit in turn.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Round in one step: look only at the digit immediately after the required place (the 1 in the thousandths) and decide once.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Multiple intermediate roundings appear; the final answer sometimes drifts (e.g. 3.15).

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops digits without placeholder zeros for large numbers — rounds 47,320 to 2sf as 47 instead of 47,000.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Keep the two significant digits (4 and 7) but preserve place with zeros so the value stays in the ten-thousands; check the size is still reasonable.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rounded large number loses its magnitude (answer is 47, not 47,000).

responseLevels.gap: Confuses sig figs with decimal places, counts leading zeros, or drops magnitude on large numbers.
responseLevels.full: Rounds accurately to a specified number of decimal places and significant figures, handles leading/trailing zeros, and chooses an appropriate degree of accuracy for a context with justification.
responseLevels.partial: Rounds to decimal places correctly but is unreliable on significant figures with leading or trailing zeros.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Round these, showing your steps. (1) 3.14159 to 2 decimal places. (2) 0.004621 to 2 significant figures. (3) 47,320 to 2 significant figures.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watch which digit the child treats as significant and how they handle the deciding digit. Decimal-place rounding and significant-figure rounding pull apart on leading zeros (task 2) and on large numbers needing placeholder zeros (task 3); a child conflating the two rules, counting leading zeros as significant, or chain-rounding will produce revealing errors.
